The firm then secured a government contract and expects to spend £530,000 on production inputs, £260,000 on overhead, and £95,000 on employee training. According to IFRS, the total amount that should be expensed is:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"£1,135,000"},{"id":"B","text":"£780,000"},{"id":"C","text":"£875,000"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct, <\/span><\/p>

Under IFRS, research expenditures are always expensed, while qualifying development costs are capitalized once feasibility and commercial viability are established. In this case:<\/span><\/p>

  • Research costs (£780,000) → expensed.<\/span><\/li>
  • Training costs (£95,000) → always expensed.<\/span><\/li>
  • Materials, labour, and production overhead relate to development → capitalized.<\/span><\/li>
  • Thus, total expense = £780,000 + £95,000 = £875,000.<\/span><\/li><\/ul>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which of the following scenarios best illustrates a liability arising from deferred revenue?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A company pays for office rent in advance, covering the next six months."},{"id":"B","text":"A business receives payment from a client for a project that will be completed next quarter"},{"id":"C","text":"An organization records an expense for utilities used during the month, though payment is scheduled for the following period."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. B is correct, <\/strong>A liability from deferred revenue occurs when a company receives payment before delivering goods or services, creating an obligation to fulfill in the future.<\/span><\/li><\/ol>


    <\/p>

    Analysis of Options:<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    • A. Paying rent in advance is a prepaid expense, not deferred revenue. (Incorrect)<\/span><\/li>
    • B. Receiving payment for a project that will be completed in the next quarter means the company has an obligation to provide the service in the future, which is deferred revenue. (Correct)<\/span><\/li>
    • C. Recording an expense for utilities used but unpaid is an accrued expense, not deferred revenue. (Incorrect)<\/span><\/li><\/ul>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which part of the statement of cash flows most closely corresponds to non-current assets reported on the balance sheet?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Financing Cash Flow"},{"id":"B","text":"Investing Cash Flow"},{"id":"C","text":"Operating Cash Flow"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is correct, <\/span><\/p>

Non-current assets on the balance sheet usually include:<\/p>

  1. <\/span>Property, plant & equipment (PPE)<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Intangible assets<\/li>
  3. <\/span>Long-term investments<\/li><\/ol>

    The cash movements related to buying\/selling these assets are reported under Investing Cash Flow.<\/p>

    Examples:<\/p>

    1. <\/span>Buying machinery → Investing outflow<\/li>
    2. <\/span>Selling equipment → Investing inflow<\/li>
    3. <\/span>Buying long-term securities → Investing outflow<\/li><\/ol>

      Why not the others?<\/h3>
      1. <\/span>Operating cash flow = day-to-day business cash (customers, suppliers, wages, etc.)<\/li>
      2. <\/span>Financing cash flow = debt, equity, dividends, borrowing\/repayment<\/li><\/ol>

        So balance sheet non-current assets connect most closely with Investing Cash Flow<\/p>"}
SearchText: Which part of the statement of cash flows most closely corresponds to non-current assets reported on the balance sheet? Financing Cash Flow Investing Cash Flow Operating Cash Flow 04.Cash Flow Statement -1

Which of the following statements is most accurate?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Capitalizing the cost will initially result in a higher net income and total assets, but will lead to lower net income in later years due to depreciation"},{"id":"B","text":"Expensing the cost will result in higher total assets and lower net income in the first year, but will improve reported profitability in later years."},{"id":"C","text":"Regardless of whether the company capitalizes or expenses the cost, operating cash flow (CFO) will remain unaffected."}]}
AnswerJson:

    Capitalizing the cost means recording it as an asset, increasing total assets and spreading the expense over multiple years through depreciation, leading to higher net income initially but lower net income in future years.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    Expensing the cost immediately reduces net income in the current year but avoids future depreciation expenses.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    (B) Incorrect – Expensing reduces assets, not increases them.<\/span><\/p>

    (C) Incorrect – Capitalizing or expensing does not impact operating cash flow (CFO) because the cash outflow is classified under investing activities, not operating activities.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"For a finance lease, which action is least likely for the lessor?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Recognize a new asset related to the lease on the balance sheet."},{"id":"B","text":"Carry a lease receivable and amortize it over the contract term."},{"id":"C","text":"Book an upfront profit at commencement in every case."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct, <\/span><\/p>

In a finance lease, the lessor removes the underlying asset and records a lease receivable that is unwound over time; that part is routine. A profit at inception is not automatic—it arises only when the consideration exceeds the asset’s carrying amount (e.g., a sales-type outcome). Thus, “recording a profit” is the least likely action because it depends on pricing versus carrying value, not merely the fact that the lease is classified as finance.<\/span><\/p>"}

If payables turnover declines from 12 to 11, and days sales outstanding increases by 4 days, what happens to the CCC?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Increases by ~1 day"},{"id":"B","text":"Increases by ~4 days"},{"id":"C","text":"Decreases by ~3 days"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

. A is correct, <\/p>

CCC = DSO + DIH − DPO<\/p>

Net change in CCC = +4 − 2.76 = +1.24 days → about +1 day. <\/p>

If initial CCC = 72 days, new CCC ≈ 73.2 days.<\/p>"}

This practice is most likely an attempt to mitigate:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Illusion of control bias"},{"id":"B","text":"Overconfidence bias."},{"id":"C","text":"Confirmation bias."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is correct, <\/span><\/p>

Illusion of control bias reflects an exaggerated belief in one’s forecasting accuracy. To counteract this, analysts often restrict inputs to variables that are proven and relevant, rather than relying on an excessive or subjective set of factors. Confirmation bias, in contrast, occurs when an analyst selectively uses evidence supporting their existing view, while overconfidence bias tends to show in underestimating uncertainty and failing to assess forecast error.<\/span><\/p>"}

AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

PresentationJson: {"stem":"For a firm operating in a perfectly competitive environment, the point at which it will most likely shut down production in the short run occurs when:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Price equals average total cost."},{"id":"B","text":"Marginal revenue equals marginal cost."},{"id":"C","text":"Marginal revenue equals average variable cost."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. C is correct, <\/span><\/li><\/ol>

AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

PresentationJson: {"stem":"According to typical labor utilization trends during the business cycle, worker productivity (output per hour worked) is most likely to be at its highest:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"At the height of an economic boom."},{"id":"B","text":"During the mid-phase of an expansion."},{"id":"C","text":"At the trough of a recession."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct, <\/span><\/p>

At the bottom of a recession, companies tend to operate with minimal staff while still striving to maximize output. This “lean production” approach means that the existing workforce is used with maximum efficiency, resulting in elevated productivity per hour worked. In contrast, productivity gains are usually less pronounced during mid-expansion or peak phases, when hiring accelerates and excess labor capacity is added.<\/span><\/p>"}

      <\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which of the following is least likely to be considered a quality of an effective central bank?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Transparency"},{"id":"B","text":"Independence"},{"id":"C","text":"Creditworthiness"}]}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which of the following best describes the role of economic indicators?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Leading indicators are useful because they track the entire economy."},{"id":"B","text":"Lagging indicators are final measures of past conditions and therefore need no revisions."},{"id":"C","text":"A mix of leading and coincident indicators can provide more effective forecasts."}]}

{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

No single indicator perfectly captures the business cycle. Leading indicators provide early signals, coincident indicators reflect current activity, and lagging indicators confirm trends. {"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

    • (A) The money supply rises, not falls.<\/span><\/li>

      <\/p>

      Therefore, short-term rates decline when defending the peg under these conditions.<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"When the central bank sells securities to commercial banks via open market operations, the most likely result is:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"An increase in bank reserves"},{"id":"B","text":"A decrease in base lending rates"},{"id":"C","text":"A decrease in banks’ capacity to lend"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. C is correct,<\/span><\/li><\/ol>

    By selling securities, the central bank withdraws reserves from the banking system. With fewer reserves, banks have less capacity to extend loans, which contracts the money supply.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    • Reserves fall, not rise, after securities are sold.<\/span><\/li>
    • Base lending rates typically rise when reserves shrink, not fall.<\/span><\/li><\/ul>

      Thus, bank lending capacity is reduced.<\/span><\/p>"}

What is most likely to happen to the housing market and the existing trade deficit?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Both increase"},{"id":"B","text":"Both decrease"},{"id":"C","text":"Housing increases, trade deficit decreases"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Following an increase in aggregate real personal income, which of the following is most likely to rise afterward?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Equity market prices"},{"id":"B","text":"Building permits for new private homes"},{"id":"C","text":"The ratio of consumer installment debt to income"}]}

{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which sequence correctly orders trading blocs by increasing degree of economic integration?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Free trade area → Economic union → Common market"},{"id":"B","text":"Customs union → Economic union → Monetary union"},{"id":"C","text":"Free trade area → Customs union → Common market"}]}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Credit cycles are least likely to:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Peak before recessions"},{"id":"B","text":"Move opposite to business cycles"},{"id":"C","text":"Magnify the length and size of business cycles"}]}

{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"An investor deposits ₹10,000 into a fund at the start of year 1. At the start of year 2, he adds ₹5,000 more. No further contributions are made. The portfolio values are ₹12,000 at the end of year 1 and ₹18,000 at the end of year 2. Which of the following statements is most accurate?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Money-weighted return is higher than time-weighted return"},{"id":"B","text":"Money-weighted return is lower than time-weighted return"},{"id":"C","text":"Money-weighted return equals time-weighted return"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is correct<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

An investor deposits ₹10,000 at the start of year 1 and ₹5,000 more at the start of year 2. The portfolio value grows to ₹12,000 at the end of year 1 and ₹18,000 at the end of year 2. To find out whether money-weighted return (MWR) is higher or lower than time-weighted return (TWR), we first solve the returns properly.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

For Year 1, the portfolio grows from ₹10,000 to ₹12,000, so the return is (12,000 – 10,000) ÷ 10,000 = 20%.<\/span><\/p>

At the start of Year 2, after adding ₹5,000 more, the new investment base is ₹12,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹17,000. By the end of Year 2, the portfolio is ₹18,000. Thus, Year 2 return is (18,000 – 17,000) ÷ 17,000 ≈ 5.88%.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Now, calculating Time-Weighted Return (TWR):<\/span><\/p>

TWR = [(1 + 0.20) × (1 + 0.0588)] – 1 = (1.20 × 1.0588) – 1 = 1.27056 – 1 = 27.056%, or about 27.06% total over two years. <\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Annualized TWR = (1.27056)^(1\/2) – 1 ≈ 12.74% per year.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

For Money-Weighted Return (MWR), we use cash flows:<\/span><\/p>

  • At time 0: cash flow = –₹10,000 (investment)<\/span><\/li>
  • At time 1: cash flow = –₹5,000 (additional investment)<\/span><\/li>
  • At time 2: cash flow = +₹18,000 (final value)<\/span><\/li><\/ul>


    <\/p>

    Using an IRR function or solving manually, the MWR comes around 10.98% per year, which is lower than 12.74% (TWR).<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    Thus, MWR is lower than TWR because most money was added before a weak return year (only ~5.88% return), diluting the performance.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which of the following statements about indifference curves is least accurate?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"They slope upward because higher risk requires higher return."},{"id":"B","text":"All points on a curve represent equal utility."},{"id":"C","text":"Indifference curves of risk-averse investors are flat lines."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Indifference curves plot combinations of expected return (E[r]) and risk (standard deviation, σ) that yield the same level of utility to an investor. For risk-averse investors, these curves are upward sloping — meaning, as risk increases, the investor demands higher return to remain equally satisfied.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

This slope reflects the trade-off between risk and return. A flat indifference curve (as stated in option C) would imply that the investor does not care about risk, which goes against the very nature of risk aversion. Risk-averse investors dislike uncertainty and require higher compensation for accepting more risk, which is why their indifference curves bend upward, not flat.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Higher indifference curves (further to the north-east) indicate higher utility i.e., more preferred combinations of risk and return. <\/span><\/p>


<\/p>","explanationMedia":{"id":"615825","url":"https:\/\/tvs.thebestlectures.in\/tvs\/Uploads\/46\/mcq_image\/08-10-2025\/a4fe5246d1c74628960f3e9bad610fd1.jpg","kind":"image"}}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the CAPM?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Investors can borrow and lend unlimited amounts at the risk-free rate."},{"id":"B","text":"Investors have heterogeneous expectations."},{"id":"C","text":"Investors are rational and utility-maximizing."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

 B is correct<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

CAPM assumes homogeneous expectations, meaning all investors process information the same way and come to identical conclusions about the investment opportunities available.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Specifically, every investor:<\/span><\/p>

Uses the same estimates for expected returns, risk (variance), and the correlation between assets.<\/span><\/p>

Believes the same probability distributions for future returns.<\/span><\/p>

Expects the same trade-off between risk and return for every asset.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Because of this, everyone selects the same optimal risky portfolio — which, when aggregated, becomes the market portfolio.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

So, under CAPM:<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Even though investors may differ in risk tolerance (which affects how much they invest in the market portfolio vs. risk-free assets),<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

They all agree on which risky portfolio is the best (the market portfolio).<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

In reality, however, investors often have different expectations due to personal biases, different information, or unique investment models — which is why real-world markets don’t fully follow this assumption.<\/span><\/p>"}

<\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"According to CAPM, if two securities have the same beta, they should:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Have the same total risk."},{"id":"B","text":"Have the same expected return, regardless of their other characteristics."},{"id":"C","text":"Be perfectly correlated."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is correct<\/span><\/p>

According to the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), the expected return on a security is determined solely by its systematic risk (beta).<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

This means:<\/span><\/p>

  • If two securities have the same beta, they are assumed to have the same expected return,<\/span><\/li>
  • Regardless of other factors like company size, industry sector, or any unique characteristics of the firms.<\/span><\/li><\/ul>


    <\/p>

    The logic is that systematic risk cannot be diversified away, so investors require compensation (in the form of higher expected return) only for the level of beta risk they bear.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    Unsystematic risks, such as business-specific or industry-specific risks, can be diversified, so CAPM assumes they do not affect the expected return.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>


    <\/p>


    <\/p>


    <\/p>


    <\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which of the following is a practical application of the CAPM in capital budgeting?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Estimating a project's future cash flows "},{"id":"B","text":"Forecasting inflation rates"},{"id":"C","text":"Determining the required rate of return to discount future cash flows"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct<\/span><\/p>

Capital budgeting is the process companies use to decide whether they should invest in long-term projects — like opening a new factory, launching a new product, or buying new equipment.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

To make this decision, companies:<\/span><\/p>

  1. Estimate the future cash flows the project will generate.<\/span><\/li>
  2. Discount those cash flows to today’s value (present value) to see if the investment is worth it.<\/span><\/li><\/ol>


    <\/p>

    But here’s the key:<\/span><\/p>

    To discount those future cash flows, they need a required rate of return — basically, the minimum return the project must earn to be worthwhile.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    That’s where CAPM comes in.<\/span><\/p>"}
SearchText: Which of the following is a practical application of the CAPM in capital budgeting? Estimating a project's future cash flows Forecasting inflation rates Determining the required rate of return to discount future cash flows 03.Portfolio Risk and Return: Part II

PresentationJson: {"stem":"An investment committee is reviewing how different behavioral errors affect portfolio decision-making. The chair emphasizes that certain belief persistence biases cause investors to cling to prior views or flawed beliefs, even in the face of contradictory evidence.  Which set of biases is most accurately classified as belief persistence biases?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Conservatism, representativeness, and hindsight biases"},{"id":"B","text":"Mental accounting, framing, and availability biases"},{"id":"C","text":"Anchoring-and-adjustment, mental accounting, and framing biases"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. <\/span>A is correct. <\/strong>Belief persistence biases occur when investors hold on to existing beliefs despite new information. These include:<\/span><\/li><\/ol>

    Conservatism bias: slow to update beliefs when presented with new evidence.<\/span><\/p>

    Representativeness bias: incorrectly judging probabilities based on stereotypes rather than statistics.<\/span><\/p>

    Hindsight bias: overestimating the predictability of past events after they occur.<\/span><\/p>

    By contrast, mental accounting, framing, availability, and anchoring-and-adjustment are information-processing biases, not belief persistence. Confirmation and illusion of control are also belief persistence biases, but anchoring is not.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>"}

security selection<\/strong> is the second step after tactical asset allocation. PresentationJson: {"stem":"The fixed rate that equates the present value of all future expected floating cash flows to the present value of fixed cash flows is termed as the:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Implied forward rate."},{"id":"B","text":"Par swap rate."},{"id":"C","text":"Zero rate."}]}

B is correct, The par swap rate is the fixed rate that makes the present value of expected floating cash flows equal to the present value of fixed cash flows. It represents the breakeven rate where an investor is indifferent between:<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"When a hedge fund enters into a reverse repurchase agreement (reverse repo), what is it most likely trying to accomplish?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Earn a higher return on idle cash balances"},{"id":"B","text":"Take a leveraged position to profit from rising security prices"},{"id":"C","text":"Borrow specific securities needed to settle a short sale"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct, <\/strong>A reverse repurchase agreement is the mirror image of a repo.<\/span><\/p>

In a normal repo, a borrower sells securities for cash and agrees to buy them back later, effectively borrowing cash.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

In a reverse repo, the hedge fund provides cash and temporarily borrows securities, agreeing to return them at a set future date and price.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Hedge funds typically use reverse repos when they have sold securities short and must deliver those securities to the buyer.<\/span><\/p>

The reverse repo lets them borrow the needed bonds or stocks while posting cash as collateral.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

It is not an interest-earning strategy (choice A) and not a way to speculate on price increases (choice B), because the repurchase price is fixed at the start and no market exposure exists beyond the short sale itself.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which statement most accurately defines the repo margin in a repurchase agreement?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"The rate of return (interest) earned by the cash lender"},{"id":"B","text":"The difference between the market value of the collateral and the cash amount loaned"},{"id":"C","text":"The extra collateral the lender demands beyond what is pledged in the repo"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct, <\/strong>The difference between the market value of the collateral and the cash amount loaned<\/span><\/p>

A repurchase agreement (repo) is effectively a short-term secured loan.<\/span><\/p>

To protect the lender against a fall in collateral value, the cash advanced is slightly less than the collateral’s current market value.<\/span><\/p>

This cushion is the repo margin (or haircut).<\/span><\/p>

It is not the repo rate, which is the interest earned on the cash lent, and it is not a request for separate or additional collateral.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>"}

{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A bond’s present value is calculated by discounting its expected cash flows using its required return (YTM). One of the assumptions underlying YTM is that the bond is held to maturity; however, this assumption may not always hold for callable bonds, which the issuer can redeem before their scheduled maturity.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Once called, a bond has no future cash flows, so its yield is calculated as though it will be called on its call date, with the call price substituted for its face value. For bonds with multiple call dates, a separate yield is calculated for each date, and each yield is referred to as the yield to first call, yield to third call, etc. The yield-to-worst is the lowest yield for all possible call dates as well as the YTM.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

In this question, the bond can be called at the end of Year 1 or Year 3. Using a financial calculator, the yields for YTM, Year 1 call, and Year 3 call are computed. The bond’s <\/span>yield to first call of 1.40%<\/strong>, which is the lowest of the three possible yields, is its yield-to-worst.<\/span><\/p>

(Choice A) <\/span>3.11%<\/strong> is the bond’s yield to maturity.<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"A bond’s current price is 102 per 100 par value. Its current yield is best described as its annual coupon payments divided by its:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"flat price."},{"id":"B","text":"full price."},{"id":"C","text":"par value."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. A is Correct, <\/strong>A bond’s yield describes and quantifies its return. There are several types of yields used for bonds. One measure is its current yield, which is the bond’s annual coupon payments divided by its flat price (i.e., the price usually quoted by dealers, which does not account for accrued interest).<\/span><\/li><\/ol>

    Current yield has two main drawbacks that limit its usefulness in analyzing or comparing bonds:<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    It accounts only for interest payments, so it ignores a bond’s capital appreciation (or loss) and is also ineffective for bonds that do not pay interest (i.e., zero-coupon bonds).<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    It fails to include accrued interest in the denominator, which has the effect of making current yield too high. A bond’s full price is its flat price plus accrued interest (Choice B).<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    (Choice C) Coupon interest divided by par value is a bond’s coupon rate.<\/span><\/p>"}

  1. A is Correct, <\/strong>Money market securities (e.g., commercial paper, Treasury bills) are short-term, highly liquid investments usually issued at a discount and redeemed at face value. Their returns can be quoted in several ways—money market yields (MMY) or bond equivalent yields (BEY)—which are calculated using the purchase price as the denominator.<\/span><\/li><\/ol>


    <\/p>

    By contrast, the quoted “discount yield” (or discount basis yield) uses the face value as the denominator. Under what reinvestment rate for coupons will the investor’s horizon yield equal the bond’s yield-to-maturity at purchase?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Lower than the bond’s YTM"},{"id":"B","text":"Equal to the bond’s YTM"},{"id":"C","text":"Higher than the bond’s YTM"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. B is Correct, <\/strong>The horizon yield is the internal rate of return on a bond investment over the investor’s actual holding period. It reflects three things:<\/span><\/li><\/ol>


    <\/p>

    The price at which the bond was bought,<\/span><\/p>

    The reinvestment rate earned on coupon payments, and<\/span><\/p>

    The price at which the bond is sold.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    If the bond is sold with no capital gain or loss (on the constant-yield price path), the horizon yield will match the original YTM only when coupons are reinvested at the same YTM.<\/span><\/p>

    If reinvested at a lower rate → horizon yield < YTM<\/span><\/p>

    If reinvested at a higher rate → horizon yield > YTM<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"A putable, fixed-rate bond is quoted with an option-adjusted spread (OAS) of 125 bp over the government spot curve. AnswerJson:

  1. A is Correct,<\/strong> Key relationship: OAS = Z-spread − Option value<\/span><\/li><\/ol>

    <\/p>

    Choice B: Misstates the benchmark. The option value is compared against the Z-spread, not the government spread.<\/span><\/p>

    <\/p>

    • Z-spread: compensates for credit + liquidity + option effects.<\/span><\/li>

AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"
  1. B is Correct, <\/strong>The bond is trading at a premium. When a premium bond is callable, the issuer is more likely to call it early (to refinance at a lower rate). If called at par, the premium is amortized over fewer years, lowering the investor’s return. The more conservative measure is therefore YTC.<\/span><\/li><\/ol>


    <\/p>

    YTC calculation:<\/strong><\/p>

    Semiannual coupon = 8%×1000\/2=40<\/span><\/p>

    Number of periods = 6×2=12.<\/span><\/p>

    Inputs: FV=1000, PMT=40, PV=−1080, N= 12 <\/span><\/p>

    Solving gives semiannual YTC ≈ 3.20%.<\/span><\/p>

    Annual YTC = 3.20% × 2 = 6.40%.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    YTM calculation:<\/strong><\/p>

    Number of periods = 12×2=24.<\/span><\/p>

    Same inputs except N=24\t<\/span><\/p>

    Solving gives semiannual YTM ≈ 3.55%.<\/span><\/p>

    Annual YTM = 3.55% × 2 = 7.10%.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>

    Because the bond is trading at a premium, YTC (6.40%) < YTM (7.10%). The conservative measure is YTC.<\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"When estimating the credit risk of a bond, which factors should be considered?","options":[{"id":"A","text":" Bond rating and recovery rate only"},{"id":"B","text":"Bond rating only"},{"id":"C","text":"Bond rating, recovery rate, and yield volatility"}]}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"At year-end, a private equity fund has returned 10% and has an 8% hurdle rate and a 20% performance fee with a catch-up clause. Based on only this information, the performance fee earned by the general partner is closest to: ","options":[{"id":"A","text":"0.00%"},{"id":"B","text":"0.40%"},{"id":"C","text":"2.00%"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C, The <\/span>catch-up clause<\/strong> allows the General Partner (GP) to receive a larger share of profits after the hurdle rate is met, until their full 20% performance fee is reached.<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Step-by-Step Calculation:<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Fund return = 10%<\/span><\/p>

Hurdle rate = 8% (LPs receive this first)<\/span><\/p>

Excess return = 10% – 8% = 2%<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Catch-up mechanism: The GP receives 100% of the next portion of profits until they reach their 20% share of total profits. <\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

GP’s share of total 10% return = 10% × 20% = 2.00%<\/span><\/p>


<\/p>

Thus, the <\/span>correct answer is C. 2.00%.<\/strong><\/p>


<\/p>


<\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which method describes how a call option is valued under the one-period binomial model?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Estimate the expected payoff at expiration using actual probabilities of up and down movements, then discount at the risk-free rate."},{"id":"B","text":"Take the simple average of the call’s payoffs at expiration and discount that figure at the risk-free rate."},{"id":"C","text":"Construct a portfolio of the call and the underlying that will have same value regardless of price of underlying at expiration."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct, The binomial model identifies a replicating portfolio consisting of the option and the underlying asset. This portfolio delivers the same value irrespective of the terminal stock price. <\/p>


<\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"If the quoted margin (QM) of a floating-rate note (FRN) is deemed to be excessive, the FRN will trade at what price relative to par value?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"At par."},{"id":"B","text":"Below par."},{"id":"C","text":"Above par."}]}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which statement about a “code of ethics” is most accurate? A code of ethics:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. does not need to include standards of conduct."},{"id":"B","text":"B.\tmust include principles-based standards of conduct."},{"id":"C","text":"C.\tmust include rules-based standards of conduct."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A code of ethics is primarily about values and broad expectations: what the profession stands for, and what kind of behavior it expects from members.<\/span><\/p>

Standards of conduct are different. They are the operational rules that translate ethics into “minimum expected behavior” in real situations (like gifts, trading priority, disclosure).<\/span><\/p>

A code of ethics may include standards of conduct, but it doesn’t have to. Many professional groups publish a values-focused code and then separately publish detailed standards.<\/span><\/p>"}

AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct, <\/strong><\/p>

Law and ethics overlap a lot, but they aren’t the same “circle.” Some actions can be legal but unethical (example: aggressively hiding fees in fine print). AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A fiduciary standard is the highest duty: it requires the professional to act in the best interests of the client, using skill and judgment, not just blindly executing requests.<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Fair dealing focuses on fairness across clients (allocation, timing, equal treatment).<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Suitability focuses on matching investments to client constraints.<\/li><\/ol>

    Fiduciary is broader: best interest + duty of care + loyalty.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson:
{"stem":"

Q. A firm introduces an ethical decision-making framework and tells employees: “Before you act, list the stakeholders, think about alternative actions, and consider second-order effects. Then decide, act, and review the outcome.”<\/p>

A framework for ethical decision making is most appropriately applied to:<\/p>.","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. aid decision makers in considering alternatives and their potential impacts."},{"id":"B","text":"B. determine whether actions are legal."},{"id":"C","text":"C. reduce the need to maintain a large compliance department."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is correct,<\/strong><\/p>

An ethical framework is not a “legal checklist.” It’s a structured thinking tool for decisions where the “right answer” may not be obvious.<\/span><\/p>

It helps you to:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>identify facts and conflicts,<\/li>
  2. <\/span>see who gets harmed\/benefited,<\/li>
  3. <\/span>explore alternatives,<\/li>
  4. <\/span>avoid “short-term win, long-term damage.”<\/li><\/ol>

    Things to remember: Ethics framework = “think clearly under pressure,” not “replace compliance.”<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"A requirement that investment professionals recommend securities that match their clients' requirements and constraints is a:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. portfolio standard."},{"id":"B","text":"B. fiduciary standard."},{"id":"C","text":"C. suitability standard."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

This is the definition of suitability: recommendations must fit the client’s constraints and requirement.<\/span><\/p>

Fiduciary is broader (best interest overall). Suitability is the matching mechanism: does this security\/strategy make sense for this client?<\/span><\/p>

Things to remember:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Suitability = “fit.”<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Fiduciary = “best interest.”<\/span><\/li><\/ol>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"A regulator studies long-term effects of unethical behavior in investing. In the long run, unethical behavior by individuals in the investment industry is most likely to:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. decrease the rate of economic growth. "},{"id":"B","text":"B. increase the overall profits of financial services firms. "},{"id":"C","text":"C. decrease financing costs for businesses."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Unethical behavior damages trust. When trust breaks:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>investors provide less capital,<\/li>
  2. <\/span>demand higher returns for risk,<\/li>
  3. <\/span>capital is allocated poorly (money goes to “best sales pitch,” not best use).<\/li><\/ol>

    That ultimately reduces productive investment and slows growth.<\/span><\/p>

    Also important: unethical behavior does not help firms long-term. It might create short-term gain, but in the long run it reduces industry profits because clients avoid the industry.<\/span><\/p>"}

{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A profession is an occupational group (e.g., doctors or lawyers) that has requirements of specialized expert knowledge, and often a focus on ethical behavior and service to the larger community or society. Q. Aarav Mehta, CFA works at Sudarshan Wealth Partners in a country where advisers follow a “suitability standard”. He recommends a product that fits the client’s long-term goals. But, if another equally suitable product exists that would pay Aarav a lower fee.<\/p>

Aarav’s conduct is best described as:<\/p>.","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. legal and ethical "},{"id":"B","text":"B. legal but unethical "},{"id":"C","text":"C. illegal and unethical"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Suitability standard: minimum legal requirement. The product must fit client constraints (risk tolerance, horizon, objectives). It does not automatically require minimizing fees or choosing the best among equals.<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Fiduciary standard: higher ethical duty. You must act in the client’s best interest. If two choices are equally suitable, the fiduciary mindset says you should avoid unnecessary client costs and avoid letting compensation distort advice.<\/li><\/ol>

    So, under a pure suitability legal regime, Aarav may be within the law. But ethically, the CFA lens expects you to recognize conflict of interest and ask:<\/span><\/p>

    “If everything else is equal, why should the client pay more just because I earn more?”<\/span><\/p>"}
SearchText: . A. legal and ethical B. legal but unethical C. illegal and unethical 01. Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession
TagsJson: [{"Key":"Chapter","Value":"01. Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession"}]

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Which is the best example of something that can be ethical but illegal?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. A whistleblower reporting corporate corruption even if local rules restrict disclosure "},{"id":"B","text":"B. An analyst trading on a tip from a company insider in the US "},{"id":"C","text":"C. A firm openly publishing its full fee structure to the public"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Laws are not the ideal means to prevent unethical behavior since they are geographically inconsistent, slow to be enacted, and subject to compliance. Financial regulations and securities laws define illegal activities. However, abiding by laws may or may not indicate ethical behavior, which extends beyond laws and includes adhering to societal expectations of right and wrong. Thus, conduct can be legal but unethical.<\/span><\/p>

Conversely, conduct can be ethical but illegal. An example of this is an act of civil disobedience, which calls attention to an unethical law yet may violate local laws. Similarly, whistle-blowers who call attention to a company's illegal activity may be violating disclosure laws. Although alerting authorities to wrongdoing is ethically correct, it may also be illegal.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"If a professional body publishes both a code of ethics and standards of conduct, the standards mainly describe:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. shared principles "},{"id":"B","text":"B. civil laws and regulations "},{"id":"C","text":"C. minimum acceptable practices and behaviors"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Code: “what we believe” (integrity, fairness, client-first mindset).<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Standards: “what you must do at minimum” to live those beliefs in real situations.<\/li><\/ol>

    Standards make ethics enforceable and practical. They translate broad values into behavior expectations, and they can be principle-based (broad) or rule-based (specific).<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"An investment professional is least likely demonstrating high professionalism when they:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. prioritize maximizing firm revenue above everything else "},{"id":"B","text":"B. stay late to support a colleague finishing a deliverable "},{"id":"C","text":"C. spend time learning and testing a new analytical method"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Professionalism in CFA context is not “working hard.” It’s working with duty. A profession exists to serve clients and society. That means you do have duties to your employer, but not at the expense of client trust and fair dealing. If your decision-making starts from “maximize my firm’s revenue,” you’re placing self-interest and employer-interest above the client-first standard that gives the profession legitimacy.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"What is the least effective method for a professional association to build trust with clients? It announces that it:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. runs a difficult qualifying exam "},{"id":"B","text":"B. operates in a highly regulated industry"},{"id":"C","text":"C. actively monitors compliance with its ethical code"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A heavily regulated industry only tells you there is external oversight. It doesn’t prove the profession itself has built a culture of integrity. Trust is stronger when it comes from within the profession:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>high entry standards (screen competence)<\/li>
  2. <\/span>monitoring and discipline (enforce integrity)<\/li>
  3. <\/span>continuing education (maintain competence)<\/li>
  4. <\/span>client focus (protect end users)<\/li><\/ol>

    So, B is least effective because it’s basically saying:<\/span><\/p>

    “Trust us because government is watching.”<\/span><\/p>

    That is weaker than:<\/span><\/p>

    “Trust us because we hold ourselves accountable.”<\/span><\/p>"}

Ethics and Trust in the Investment Profession

PresentationJson: {"stem":"The best reason trust is needed in the investment profession is that investment managers can:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. deliver greater value to society "},{"id":"B","text":"B. increase the profession’s prestige "},{"id":"C","text":"C. control client decisions more strongly"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

CFA frames investment management as an industry that influences: savings, retirement, capital allocation, and corporate governance.<\/span><\/p>

If clients don’t trust investment professionals, they withdraw participation, allocate less capital, demand higher returns, and the cost of capital rises. That hurts real economic outcomes.<\/span><\/p>

Yes, trust can increase prestige or influence. But CFA always asks:<\/span><\/p>

“What’s the most appropriate reason?”<\/span><\/p>

The correct answer is the one that benefits society and market functioning, not ego or control.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"If you want to lower the chance that your decision creates ethical problems you didn’t anticipate, the most useful tool is:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. the profession’s code of ethics. "},{"id":"B","text":"B. the standards of conduct. "},{"id":"C","text":"C. an ethical decision-making framework."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A framework forces you to systematically identify stakeholders, facts (even uncomfortable ones), conflicts, alternatives, and consequences, and then assess outcomes after acting. That structured thinking is exactly what reduces “blind spots.” A code and standards guide behavior, but they’re not designed as a step-by-step decision tool for mapping consequences.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"The investment profession most effectively builds and sustains trust by:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. pushing for harsher legal punishment for violations. "},{"id":"B","text":"B. setting standards that are identical to regulatory rules. "},{"id":"C","text":"C. ensuring professionals communicate investment traits accurately to clients."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Trust is built when clients feel they are treated fairly and can make informed decisions. Clear, truthful communication about returns, risks, fees, and product characteristics is a direct expression of integrity and client focus. More penalties or matching regulators doesn’t automatically create trust; trust comes from professionals’ conduct and the profession’s culture.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"When unethical behavior happens, overconfidence bias is least likely to cause someone to overestimate:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. how ethical their own actions are. "},{"id":"B","text":"B. how “pure” or well-intentioned their motives are. "},{"id":"C","text":"C. how much external pressures influence their behavior."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Overconfidence usually makes people think: “I’m more ethical than others” and “my intentions are good,” so they overrate their own morality and motives. But when it comes to situational forces like money, prestige, culture, boss pressure, people typically underestimate how much these external factors shape behavior. That’s why C is the least likely thing they overestimate.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"CFA Institute Professional Conduct staff (PCS) concludes that Rohan Mehta, CFA violated the Standards. He refuses to accept PCS’s proposed sanctions. What happens next?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"A. PCS immediately revokes his charter. "},{"id":"B","text":"B. PCS issues him a cautionary letter and closes the file. "},{"id":"C","text":"C. A panel of the Disciplinary Review Committee reviews PCS’s investigative report."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

The CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program is a framework for handling inquiries about members' and candidates' professional conduct. The Professional Conduct staff (PCS) initiates an inquiry, which is based on an external complaint or internal investigations. The PCS may question the accused member or anyone else associated with the inquiry. The PCS records evidence relevant to the investigation, prepares a report, and determines if a violation occurred.<\/span><\/p>

If the PCS believes that a violation occurred and the member accepts this finding, then the PCS will either issue a cautionary letter or proceed with disciplinary action. If the accused rejects the finding, then a panel of the Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC) becomes involved. The panel reviews the PCS's report and further investigates the matter. The DRC determines whether a violation occurred and sets the final disciplinary action.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"When advising a client, members and candidates must decide investment suitability based only on:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"the strengths of the single investment being recommended. AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

CFA Members (including CFA charterholders) and Candidates are obligated to abide by and advocate for the Code of Ethics (i.e. the Code) and the Standards of Professional Conduct (i.e. the Standards), which provide guidance for appropriate ethical behavior. The Code includes general principles to which Members and Candidates must adhere. In contrast, the Standards address the principles' more specific applications, which must be followed.<\/span><\/p>

Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the Members' and Candidates' responsibilities to assess the suitability of investments for each client. A Member or Candidate does this by researching each client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance, which are compared to the characteristics of each proposed investment. Specifically, a Member or Candidate must determine suitability based on a client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before taking investment action.<\/span><\/p>"}

The Code is aspirational, and one of its key principles is that members\/candidates should not only maintain their own competence, but also support the competence of others in the profession. That pushes the profession upward over time.<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson:
{"stem":"

An investment firm, Suryodaya Asset Partners, operates through subsidiaries in India, Singapore, and the UAE. Each subsidiary is legally registered under a different company name, but all of them market themselves to clients under one common brand: “Suryodaya”.<\/p>

When defining the firm for GIPS compliance, which subsidiaries should Suryodaya most appropriately include?<\/p>.","options":[{"id":"A","text":"All subsidiaries operating under the same brand name "},{"id":"B","text":"Only the subsidiaries using the exact legal name “Suryodaya Asset Partners” "},{"id":"C","text":"Only the subsidiaries located in the country where the firm is seeking compliance"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Under GIPS, the starting point is not performance calculation—it is defining “the firm” properly. If the firm definition is narrow or selective, everything else becomes misleading because the firm can “pick” which entities count and which do not.<\/span><\/p>

GIPS pushes firms to adopt the broadest reasonable definition of the firm, especially when operations span multiple countries. The logic is simple:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>A prospective client thinks they are evaluating the track record of the brand they know.<\/li>
  2. <\/span>If the firm excludes a subsidiary that operates under the same brand, the client may be seeing a partial story, not the full organization’s investment activity.<\/li>
  3. <\/span>Firm-wide definition also affects total firm assets and composite construction, which must represent how the firm truly manages money across that brand.<\/li><\/ol>

    So, even if the legal names differ, if they operate under the same brand name, they should be included in the firm definition for GIPS compliance.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Trishul Investment Managers is building composites for GIPS reporting. Which of the following is least likely to be a GIPS requirement when constructing a composite?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Every composite must contain at least two discretionary portfolios "},{"id":"B","text":"A portfolio’s inclusion in a composite must be decided ex ante (before performance is known)"},{"id":"C","text":"All actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios must be included in at least one composite"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A composite is meant to represent a strategy (like “Indian large-cap growth” or “short duration debt”) through actual portfolios managed that way.<\/span><\/p>

What GIPS is trying to prevent is the classic manipulation: “Let’s show only the best accounts and call that our strategy performance.”<\/span><\/p>

That’s why GIPS requires two big disciplines:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>All actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios must be in at least one composite. This prevents selective omission of real client portfolios. <\/li>
  2. <\/span>Composite membership must be ex ante. Meaning you decide the inclusion rules before you know which accounts will look good. This blocks cherry-picking after the fact. <\/li><\/ol>

    A composite can have just one portfolio if that strategy is unique to that single portfolio. So “minimum two portfolios” is not a requirement. <\/span><\/p>


    <\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"What best describes the fundamental purpose of the GIPS standards for firms?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"To present a firm’s investment performance fully, fairly, and ethically "},{"id":"B","text":"To act as a global regulatory authority that settles performance reporting disputes "},{"id":"C","text":"To set a minimum reporting threshold that becomes valid only after mandatory third-party verification"}]}

{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

GIPS exists because performance reporting can easily be manipulated without strict consistency. The standards are built on the ethical foundation that performance should be shown with:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Fair representation (not selective or misleading)<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Full disclosure (so clients understand what they’re seeing)<\/li>
  3. <\/span>Comparable reporting across firms (so prospects can evaluate managers properly)<\/li><\/ol>

    So, the purpose is not “minimum disclosure,” and it is not a regulation enforced by a government body. It is a global, ethical framework for presenting performance in a way that maintains trust in markets. <\/span><\/p>

    Also, verification is considered best practice but is not mandatory, so it cannot be the defining purpose.<\/span><\/p>"}

According to the Fundamentals of Compliance provision of the GIPS, to claim compliance a firm must adhere to all GIPS requirements. This is accomplished only if the entire firm follows all mandated rules.<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"If a firm elects to verify its GIPS compliance, which statement is most accurate?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Verification is mandatory every year"},{"id":"B","text":"Verification must cover all composites of the firm "},{"id":"C","text":"Verification guarantees each composite is perfectly accurate in every detail"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Verification, if done, is not meant to be selective. It examines whether the firm:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>constructed composites according to GIPS rules, and<\/li>
  2. <\/span>has a compliant process for calculating and presenting performance.<\/li><\/ol>

    Because the claim is firm-wide, verification logically must address the firm’s composite framework across the board, not a handpicked subset.<\/span><\/p>

    Verification is recommended but not required.<\/span><\/p>

    Verification increases confidence in the process, but it does not promise that every figure is flawless or that a composite is “accurate” in the absolute sense. It’s more about compliance with required methods and procedures.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Saffron Capital acquires Kaveri Asset Management. Both historically claimed GIPS compliance. Saffron retains Kaveri’s portfolio managers, but most of Kaveri’s research\/support team is not retained; Saffron’s team will now do research. Can Saffron “link” Kaveri’s past performance to its own GIPS history?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"No "},{"id":"B","text":"Yes, because an acquisition occurred "},{"id":"C","text":"Yes, because the portfolio managers are still there"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Linking past performance is allowed only if the investment decision-making capability and process are substantially carried forward without a meaningful break. It’s not just “same brand” or “same portfolio managers.”<\/span><\/p>

GIPS looks for conditions like:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>substantially all key decision-makers are retained (not only PMs, but also the supporting research function that influences decisions),<\/li>
  2. <\/span>decision-making process remains largely intact and independent,<\/li>
  3. <\/span>records exist to support the historical numbers, and<\/li>
  4. <\/span>there is no break in the performance record.<\/li><\/ol>

    Here, losing most of the research\/support staff means the “decision engine” changed materially. So linking is not appropriate.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Under GIPS fundamentals of compliance, what are the two key definitions a firm must establish?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"The firm definition and what counts as “discretion” "},{"id":"B","text":"Prospective clients and the firm definition "},{"id":"C","text":"Discretion and prospective clients"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Two definitions drive everything that comes after:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Define the “firm”: GIPS wants the firm boundary set broadly so the firm can’t exclude certain offices\/subsidiaries and only show the best-performing parts. A broad firm definition supports fair reporting of total assets and composites.<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Define “discretion”: Composites generally include discretionary portfolios because they reflect manager skill. If discretion isn’t defined clearly, firms can inconsistently include\/exclude portfolios, which again creates room for manipulation.<\/li><\/ol>

    Prospective clients aren’t something you “define” for compliance. They are recipients of required reporting, but not a definitional cornerstone like firm and discretion.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"A firm wants to describe how it qualifies to claim GIPS compliance. Which statement is most appropriate?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"“We calculate returns in accordance with GIPS.” "},{"id":"B","text":"“We assign portfolios to composites using pre-set (ex-ante) rules.” "},{"id":"C","text":"“We exclude composites that are under five years old.”"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

A key GIPS safeguard is ex ante composite inclusion. The firm must decide the inclusion rules before seeing performance for the period. This blocks “after the fact” exclusion of weak accounts.<\/span><\/p>

So, the most meaningful compliant idea here is: composite membership is driven by pre-established criteria, not by performance outcomes.<\/span><\/p>

GIPS is strict about how firms describe compliance. Saying “we calculate in accordance with GIPS” can be considered misleading because GIPS compliance is about full presentation and firm-wide requirements, not just a calculation claim.<\/span><\/p>

Newer composites must generally be shown since inception (if under five years). Excluding them would violate the fair representation objective.<\/span><\/p>"}

{"stem":"

Ananya Iyer, CFA, manages two pooled vehicles at the same firm: Sundar Equity Mutual Fund and Arjuna Long-Short Fund (hedge fund). After research, she decides FilterBrew Pvt Ltd fits both funds. She places a limit order for 1,00,000 shares at ₹2,900 and tells the broker to allocate 90% to the mutual fund and 10% to the hedge fund, consistent with mandate\/size.<\/p>

That day, FilterBrew announces a major patent, and the price jumps quickly. The broker fills only 10,000 shares. After seeing the jump, Ananya changes her mind and tells the broker to allocate all 10,000 shares to the hedge fund, then cancels the remaining order.<\/p>

Does Ananya most likely comply with Standard III(B) Fair Dealing?<\/p>.","options":[{"id":"A","text":"No, because she favored one client over another after new information. "},{"id":"B","text":"Yes, because the hedge fund got a full allocation, but not more. "},{"id":"C","text":"Yes, because a pro-rata fill would be too small to matter."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Under Fair Dealing, the “client” is each fund, and you must treat them fairly and objectively in investment actions and allocations.<\/span><\/p>

The key violation is changing the allocation only after learning the price moved up. Once Ananya knows the trade is “lucky” (price jump), she redirects the benefit to the hedge fund and blocks the mutual fund from participating in gains it was originally entitled to. That’s classic unfair dealing.<\/span><\/p>

The clean approach here was simple: since the order was partially filled, stick to the pre-stated allocation method (often pro-rata, unless a documented minimum-lot policy applies and was disclosed upfront).<\/span><\/p>"}

Meera Menon, CFA, is an independent consultant. Her clients include the investment portfolio of SBI Life Insurance and the personal account of that portfolio’s manager, Rohit Jain. Meera is contacted by the CFA Institute’s Professional Conduct Program (PCP) about Meera’s own conduct (unethical but not illegal). "},{"id":"B","text":"Both SBI’s portfolio and Rohit’s personal account. "},{"id":"C","text":"Neither account."}]}

{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Confidentiality applies to everyone: individuals and institutions.<\/span><\/p>

Standard III(E) allows disclosure when: (1) illegal client activity, (2) required by law, or (3) client permits. There’s an additional important point used in ethics questions: when local law permits, members\/candidates must cooperate with PCP investigations, including providing client information PCP requests in an investigation involving the member\/candidate. Here, local law doesn’t prohibit it, and there is no illegal client activity issue blocking disclosure. So, the most appropriate response is to provide the requested information for both clients to PCP.<\/span><\/p>"}

Which action(s) most likely comply with Standard V(C) Record Retention?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Only saving other research documentation "},{"id":"B","text":"Publishing a new report at the new firm using public\/new research "},{"id":"C","text":"Both"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

The Standard requires you (and the firm) to maintain supporting records for analyses and recommendations. That includes “new media” like emails, texts, and social media posts when they are used as inputs to your analysis.<\/span><\/p>

Arjun’s report creation itself can be fine because he is producing a new report at a new employer using public information\/new research, not walking away with proprietary employer files. So, publishing can comply.<\/span><\/p>

But he fails the record retention requirement by not retaining the social media\/blog content he relied on. Public availability doesn’t remove the duty to maintain an audit trail supporting what you used at that time. Posts can be edited\/deleted; you still need evidence.<\/span><\/p>"}

Under Standard I(C) Misrepresentation:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"No violation occurred "},{"id":"B","text":"Only Aditi violated "},{"id":"C","text":"Both Aditi and Raheem violated"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Misrepresentation includes omission and presenting information in a way that misleads. Composite reporting is a high-risk area because excluding accounts can “clean up” performance.<\/span><\/p>

The moment they remove accounts outside a defined, consistently applied policy, they are effectively cherry-picking and misrepresenting what clients should understand as strategy performance.<\/span><\/p>

Raheem is not “safe” just because the root cause was software. Ethics cares about what you present: the revised composite becomes incomplete and misleading.<\/span><\/p>

Aditi violates because she creates and distributes the misleading report. Raheem violates because he pressures and participates in the decision to mislead.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Karan Mehta, CFA, at AlphaBridge Research reads a detailed blog post about Pragati Bank Ltd that contains unique drivers of growth. His colleague Nisha Rao, CFA, proofreads and later adds a chart from the RBI publication, properly citing RBI. Under the Code and Standards:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Both Karan and Nisha violated "},{"id":"B","text":"Karan violated, Nisha did not "},{"id":"C","text":"Nisha violated, Karan did not"}]}

{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Plagiarism isn’t only copying exact sentences. If the substance\/structure of the idea is taken from someone else and presented as your own, that’s plagiarism unless you clearly attribute.<\/span><\/p>

Karan’s “I changed wording + timeline” is not enough. He is still borrowing the blogger’s intellectual contribution (the “fresh insights”) without credit.<\/span><\/p>

Has Kavya violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Yes"},{"id":"B","text":"No, because she knows Kapoor personally "},{"id":"C","text":"No, because the FoHF does diligence for investors"}]}

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

V(A) requires a reasonable and adequate basis supported by research. Past friendship and good returns are not a substitute for due diligence.<\/span><\/p>

Even when investing via a FoHF, you still need to do diligence appropriate to the product. At a minimum: understand strategy, risks, fees, governance, transparency, liquidity gates, and how the FoHF selects\/monitors underlying funds.<\/span><\/p>

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Rituja Sharma, CFA, and Farhan Qureshi (Level I candidate) work in wealth management at Sahyog Bank. Rituja learns Farhan receives referral payments from the bank’s brokerage team tied to commissions, but he hides it from clients and even from the firm. Rituja checks local rules and believes it’s illegal. She reports it to her supervisor, but nothing changes and Farhan continues. What is Rituja’s most appropriate next step under Standard I(A)?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Resign immediately "},{"id":"B","text":"Request transfer to another department of the bank "},{"id":"C","text":"Stay and gather stronger evidence"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard I(A) says: understand and comply with law; if violations occur, you must not participate and must dissociate from the misconduct.<\/span><\/p>

The usual sequence: report internally first (she did), then if unresolved, dissociate. Dissociation often means requesting reassignment, refusing involvement, and ensuring you aren’t supporting the activity.<\/span><\/p>

Resignation can be required if you cannot dissociate, but it’s not always the immediate first move.<\/span><\/p>

Staying to collect evidence keeps you connected to an activity you believe is illegal, increasing risk you’re seen as assisting or tolerating it.<\/span><\/p>"}

Vikram Malhotra, CFA, runs Lotus Equities, focused on small caps. Marketing materials show “average compounded returns” over 5\/10\/15 years. They disclose:<\/p>

• Returns include both active and closed accounts.<\/p>

• Returns are shown gross of management fees.<\/p>

Has Vikram violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation with respect to these materials?<\/p>.","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Yes, due to missing termination dates "},{"id":"B","text":"Yes, due to gross-of-fees reporting "},{"id":"C","text":"Yes, due to both issues"}]}

{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard III(D) requires performance to be fair, accurate, and complete. You can include terminated accounts (you should), but you must present it in a way that doesn’t mislead.<\/span><\/p>

If you include terminated accounts but don’t show when they were terminated, readers cannot judge survivorship effects or understand account history. That missing context can mislead.<\/span><\/p>

Showing gross-of-fees is allowed as long as it’s clearly stated. There is no requirement here to list the fee amount inside marketing pieces, as long as gross vs net is clear.<\/span><\/p>"}

<\/p>Who most likely violates Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Only Kapoor "},{"id":"B","text":"Only Sood "},{"id":"C","text":"Both Kapoor and Sood"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

c is coirrect,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard I(B) is about protecting judgment. You must not offer, solicit, or accept gifts\/benefits that could reasonably be expected to compromise independence and objectivity, or even create that appearance.<\/span><\/p>

Kapoor’s conduct: Offering luxury match hospitality to someone who can influence a business decision (platform inclusion) is effectively an attempt to influence Sood’s judgment. Even if she calls it “networking,” the context makes it a potential inducement.<\/span><\/p>

Sood’s conduct: He rejects the gift, which is good. But then he redirects the request into a different form: “Buy pricey fundraiser tickets so we can talk business.” That is a solicitation tied to a business benefit. When the “donation” is linked to access and allocation decisions, it becomes an independence\/objectivity issue.<\/span><\/p>

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Not every gift is a violation. Standard I(B) focuses on whether a gift could reasonably be expected to compromise independence\/objectivity.<\/span><\/p>

Here, the gift is from a client as appreciation for service already provided. That is different from gifts from issuers, brokers, or vendors who might be trying to influence your research ratings or trade flow. A client gift can be acceptable when:<\/span><\/p>

  2. <\/span>it is not so large or frequent that it becomes an inducement, and<\/li>
  3. <\/span>it does not pressure the adviser to treat that client unfairly versus others.<\/li><\/ol>

    Deshmukh did the right step by reporting it to compliance, creating transparency. B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard III(B) requires fair and objective treatment of clients. When allocations are limited (especially IPOs), you must use a consistent method that does not unfairly favor certain accounts.<\/span><\/p>

Key principles here:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Your mother’s account is still a client account, and if she is suitable for the IPO, she can participate like other clients.<\/li>

Under Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, Aman’s action:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"cannot be a violation because clients agreed to the practice  "},{"id":"B","text":"cannot be a violation because hot IPOs can always be divided fairly  "},{"id":"C","text":"may still be a violation even though clients agreed"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Client approval does not automatically make something ethical under CFA Standards. The rule is simple: client transactions must come before personal transactions. In a “hot issue,” supply is limited. If Aman participates, he is reducing the number of shares available for clients — even if he “splits equally.” This creates a situation where Aman’s personal benefit might come at the cost of client preference. PresentationJson: {"stem":"Aditya Khanna, CFA, is an analyst at Axis Securities. The company is going to announce a sell recommendation on Biocon stock in one hour. According to the Code and Standards, trading on Khanna's wife's account can begin:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"only after Khanna, as a beneficial owner, has given an appropriate amount of time for clients and his employer to act.  "},{"id":"B","text":"only after the recommendation is announced to the general public.  "},{"id":"C","text":"as soon as the information is disseminated to all clients."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Family accounts that are client accounts should be treated like any other firm account and should neither be given special treatment nor be disadvantaged because of an existing family relationship with the member or candidate. Members or candidates may undertake transactions in accounts for which they are a beneficial owner only after their clients and employers have had adequate opportunity to act on the recommendation. Personal transactions include those made for the member or candidate's own account, for family (including spouse, children, and other immediate family members) accounts, and for accounts in which the member or candidate has a direct or indirect pecuniary interest, such as a trust or retirement account. It could be argued that Khanna is a beneficial owner of his wife's account and the reason why his wife's account should be treated like any other client account is because it does not state that Khanna makes the trades in his wife's account. From that we are to infer that another person other than Khanna is managing his wife's account thus she should be treated like any other client.<\/span><\/p>"}

"},{"id":"B","text":"inform her supervisor of her discovery.  "},{"id":"C","text":"notify potential investors of the omission on a fair and equitable basis."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Roy is in possession of material nonpublic information, and her most appropriate course of action is to inform her supervisor (or the firm's compliance officer) of what she has learned. Underwriters and investment bankers routinely possess material nonpublic information about their client firms, and it is acceptable to share this information within the department when doing so is necessary to carry out an issuance of the client firm's securities. If Roy's firm determines that the information affects the value of the debentures, they must revise and recirculate the prospectus. Failing to do so may violate Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. Not informing her employer may be detrimental to her firm's interests and reputation if proceeding with the new issue without disclosure would violate regulations or laws. Roy may not, however, share the material nonpublic information with prospective buyers, or with anyone in her firm outside the underwriting department.<\/span><\/p>"}

Arjun first buys a large quantity of shares in a low-liquidity microcap mining stock. After that, he posts online that he has taken a “big position” in the stock. Then he spreads a message saying: “Strong sources suggest this company may get acquired at a huge premium very soon.”<\/p>

AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Here’s the key point:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Arjun did not just “share an opinion.”<\/span><\/li>
  2. <\/span>He created a false acquisition rumor, knowing it would push the stock up.<\/span><\/li>
  3. <\/span>This is a classic pump-and-dump strategy: Buy cheap, Hype it with misleading info, Price will rise, Sell into the buying pressure.<\/span><\/li><\/ol>

Rohan Singh, CFA is responsible for allotting shares of an IPO to clients who have discretionary portfolios.<\/p>

He takes advice from colleagues:<\/p>

  1. <\/span>Neha Verma says: “Check every client’s Investment Policy Statement (IPS) before allocating.”<\/li>
  2. <\/span>Aman Bhatia says: “Give shares in proportion to each client’s AUM.”<\/li>
  3. <\/span>Kunal Arora says: “Give equal number of IPO shares to every client.”<\/li><\/ol> To comply with Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, whose suggestion is most appropriate?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Neha Verma "},{"id":"B","text":"Aman Bhatia "},{"id":"C","text":"Kunal Arora"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard III(B) Fair Dealing means clients must be treated fairly and objectively.<\/span><\/p>

“Fair” does NOT mean “equal.”<\/span><\/p>

The best method is:<\/span><\/p>

  1. <\/span>Review each client’s IPS<\/span><\/li>
  2. <\/span>Allocate in a way that matches each client’s: objectives, constraints, and suitability.<\/span><\/li><\/ol>

    So, Neha’s approach is strongest, because it ensures allocation is aligned with client needs.<\/span><\/p>"}

AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Recommendations for compliance with the Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors acknowledge that a supervisor may not be able to dictate the ethical standards, culture, or compliance efforts of an entire firm, but should work with management to encourage the adoption of effective compliance tools. <\/span><\/p>

One effective compliance tool is an incentive structure that supports ethical behavior.<\/span><\/p>

Here, Pandey should have recognized the firm's incentive structure as not supportive of ethical behavior and, in fact, perhaps as actually encouraging unethical behavior. She should have brought this weakness to her supervisor's attention rather than accepting it without question. <\/span><\/p>

The guidance for Standard IV(C) is very clear that failing to detect unethical behavior does not mean that the supervisor violated the Standard or ignored its recommendations. <\/span><\/p>

However, in this case, there is no evidence that Pandey ever investigated the firm's policies and procedures to determine if they were adequate to prevent the type of unethical behavior that occurred.
