Karan Malhotra is a Level I CFA Candidate working for a large Indian charity foundation called “Sahyog Trust.” His job is to invest the charity’s surplus funds prudently. Recently, due to the sudden retirement of the Trust’s CFO, Karan has been asked to temporarily support additional responsibilities in:<\/p>

  1. <\/span>internal audit work<\/li>
  2. <\/span>management accounting reporting<\/li>
  3. <\/span>operational finance tasks<\/li><\/ol>

    Because of this workload, Karan has much less time to do deep research. To follow the Trust’s equity allocation policy quickly, Karan invests in a popular broad-based Nifty 50 index fund, without doing deep security-level evaluation.<\/p>

    Separately, Karan is also an activist in a community group protesting a government hospital’s decision to shut down a local emergency unit. During weekend protests, Karan has been arrested twice for civil disobedience.<\/p> Based on this information, has Karan most likely violated Standard I(D) Misconduct?","options":[{"id":"A","text":"No "},{"id":"B","text":"Yes, because being arrested is illegal activity "},{"id":"C","text":"Yes, because he did not research the index fund properly"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard I(D) Misconduct is primarily concerned with the professional activities of a Member or Candidate, which covers all conduct that may negatively impact the Member's or Candidate's trustworthiness, reputation, or ability to perform their duties. Examples include acts that involve lying, cheating, theft, fraud, or other dishonest behavior. However, violations of Standard I(D) are not limited to actions specifically prohibited by the Standard.<\/span><\/p>

Failure to take appropriate action or lack of sufficient effort may also constitute a violation. However, there are other Standards that specifically address Karan's adding the broad-based equity fund (e.g. V(A) – Diligence and Reasonable Basis; III(C) – Suitability). Standard I(D) addresses fraud and misconduct that erode public trust in the profession. Nothing in Karan's actions suggests that he committed fraud or deception, and asserting that Karan also violated Standard I(D) is an overbroad reading of the Standard.<\/span><\/p>

Being arrested and jailed for acts of civil disobedience does not in itself constitute a violation of Standard I(D). In this case, Karan's protest activities are a form of civil disobedience that does not reflect poorly on his professional capacities.<\/span><\/p>"}

Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to encourage behavior that complies with local laws, rules established by their firms, and the Code and Standards. Any Member or Candidate who cannot perform supervisory responsibilities due to these shortcomings should decline to accept supervisory responsibility, in writing, until the compliance system is improved and allows for adequate controls. PresentationJson: {"stem":"When a firm possesses material, nonpublic information about a stock, the least appropriate policy is a suspension of all:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"risk-arbitrage activity in the stock by the firm. "},{"id":"B","text":"market-making activity in the stock by the firm.  "},{"id":"C","text":"personal trading in the stock by firm employees."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard II Integrity of Capital Markets discusses the member's and candidate's responsibility to protect the integrity of the capital markets. Standard II(A) focuses specifically on the use of material nonpublic information.<\/span><\/p>

Trading with material nonpublic information (\"insider trading\") threatens market integrity, which relies on all market participants having fair access to information and no participant having the advantage of using information that is not widely available.<\/span><\/p>

When a firm has material nonpublic information about a stock, it must try to ensure that trading does not violate the Standard. A ban on all trading in the stock is not always necessary or advisable. For example, if a firm acts as a market maker or dealer for a certain security, suspension of market making may signal that the firm has material nonpublic information and, in effect, expose that information. Market-making activities may continue but should be restricted to taking passive, counterparty positions in unsolicited trades.<\/span><\/p>"}
SearchText: When a firm possesses material, nonpublic information about a stock, the least appropriate policy is a suspension of all: risk-arbitrage activity in the stock by the firm. market-making activity in the stock by the firm. personal trading in the stock by firm employees. 03. Guidance for Standards I–VII

{"stem":"

Kangana Kumawat, CFA, investor relations manager at Adami Enterprises, arranges a video conference call with a small group of sell-side analysts to discuss confidential company developments. On the call, Kumawat tells the analysts that Adami Enterprises has decided to selectively disclose information to give the analysts time to think about the company developments before they are publicly announced in two days. Kumawat then tells the analysts that the company had a disagreement with its auditors over revenue recognition policies and as a result, Adami Enterprises has changed auditors.<\/p>

Bharat Vyas, CFA, is an analyst on the call and immediately recognizes the negative implications this will have for Adami Enterprises. Vyas believes a potential accounting scandal will not only drive down the stock price, but will motivate customers to switch to Relanc Industries, Adami Enterprises largest competitor. Later that day, Vyas calls his best clients and recommends purchase of Relanc Industries without mentioning Adami Enterprises. Numerous clients act on this recommendation.<\/p> According to Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, it is most likely that:","options":[{"id":"A","text":"no violation occurred. "},{"id":"B","text":"only Kumawat violated the Standard. "},{"id":"C","text":"only Vyas violated the Standard."}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["C"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information requires Members and Candidates to abstain from investment actions if they have material nonpublic information (MNPI). Trading on or acting on MNPI erodes the public's trust in the fairness of the capital markets. MNPI can come from many sources, and a Member or Candidate must evaluate information to decide whether it is MNPI before acting on it.<\/span><\/p>

Selective disclosure (e.g. analysts on a conference call, corporate insiders) does not necessarily make information public. In this question, Kangana Kumawat and Adami Enterprises intentionally disclosed information and gave the analysts the timeline of when that information would be publicly disseminated. This type of selective disclosure is not a violation of the Standard.<\/span><\/p>

However, by agreeing to be part of the select group receiving the information, Bharat Vyas has a duty to keep this information confidential until it is released publicly by the company. Even though Vyas did not directly disclose the MNPI, he violated the Standard by using his knowledge of MNPI to influence others to act based on this information. Acting on MNPI is not limited strictly to that company's securities (e.g. Adami Enterprises), any trading based on MNPI is a violation of the Standard.<\/span><\/p>"}

PresentationJson: {"stem":"Ananya Iyer, CFA, is an analyst at a firm that has not adopted GIPS but follows the CFA Institute Code and Standards as its ethical guidelines. The firm is preparing a client-facing performance report for its equity strategy. To comply with Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Iyer should most likely advise the firm to: ","options":[{"id":"A","text":"disclose whether results are reported gross of fees or net of fees.  "},{"id":"B","text":"show performance using a single “representative” account.  "},{"id":"C","text":"remove terminated accounts from the results to avoid “distortions.”"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["A"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

A is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard III(D) is about one thing: don’t let performance reporting become marketing by omission. Even if a firm hasn’t adopted GIPS, the output still has to be fair, accurate, and complete.<\/span><\/p>

In this case, the biggest “completeness” gap is fees. A return number without clarifying gross vs. net can mislead a reader because the investor’s experience depends on fees. So, the cleanest compliance step is: explicitly disclose gross-of-fees vs net-of-fees reporting.<\/span><\/p>

Why the other options are not correct:<\/span><\/p>

Option B (single representative account) is risky because it can cherry-pick. Best practice is to show a composite of similar portfolios, not one account that “looks nice.”<\/span><\/p>

Option C (exclude terminated accounts) is also problematic. Dropping accounts that were closed (often after poor results) can quietly inflate reported performance and makes results incomplete.<\/span><\/p>"}

C is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard IV(A) says you should act for the benefit of your employer. But it also assumes you’re acting within the boundaries of law and market integrity. When an employer’s instruction crosses into illegal or market-damaging behavior, loyalty has limits.<\/span><\/p>

Kunal Deshpande, CFA, runs a hedge fund and holds a short position in Trishul Engineering Ltd (TEL). TEL’s stock keeps rising, and Kunal wants to exit without taking a loss. The negative publicity pushes the stock down, and Kunal closes the short profitably.<\/p>

","options":[{"id":"A","text":"Jha only "},{"id":"B","text":"Deshpande only "},{"id":"C","text":"Both Jha and Deshpande"}]}
AnswerJson:
{"correct":["B"],"marks":1.00,"negative":0.00,"explanation":"

B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

Standard II(B) is about intent. The Standard is violated when a person uses information or transactions to distort price or volume with the intent to mislead.<\/span><\/p>

Kunal clearly commits information-based manipulation. He spreads false “company trouble” narratives specifically to push the stock down so he can profit from his short. That is textbook manipulation under II(B). <\/span><\/p>

Manisha, on the other hand, is trading for legitimate personal reasons: diversification and liquidity. She is not trying to mislead the market or manufacture price movement. Even if she suspects the market is reacting to false rumors, simply trading in a market where misinformation exists is not automatically a violation. B is Correct,<\/strong><\/p>

    Why not small-cap?<\/span><\/p>

    Because there is no change. Standard V(B) is not asking you to re-explain stable strategies every time operations change. The trigger is a material shift in process.<\/span><\/p>"}
